newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Falling prices hit Australian nickel giant's profits.
newsitem.headline: Falling prices hit Australian nickel giant's profits.

text.p: Sliding nickel prices have cut half-year earnings for one of the world's biggest producers of the metal, but Australia's WMC Ltd said on Wednesday a recovery has already begun.

The company unveiled a net profit for the six months to December 31 of A$100.7 million ($76 million), a fall of 46 percent from a year ago. It attributed the widely anticipated slide to low commodity prices and a higher Australian dollar.
"The main overwhelming factor is the leverage that the company has to both prices and exchange rates...," WMC managing director Hugh Morgan told a news conference.
By far the biggest dent in profits came from nickel division earnings, which more than halved to A$64.4 million.
WMC blamed the slump on substantially lower realised nickel prices and a strong Australian dollar which offset a rise in production.

Nickel was hobbled last year by poor demand from the stainless steel producers, which account for two-thirds of Western world nickel consumption. WMC's nickel division was also hit in the first half by an A$8.4 million ($6.4 million) workforce restructuring charge.
But asked by reporters how the company's second half would compare with the first, Morgan said: "Markedly better".
He forecast higher nickel prices and a more favourable exchange rate, as well as higher production and lower costs.
Morgan was confident nickel production costs per unit would be cut by 10 percent by the company's year-end.
"We should get our 10 percent reduction by the 30th of June," Morgan told a news conference.
WMC announced the cost-cutting target late last year, but analysts have been sceptical about WMC's ability to meet it.

The market, which had pummelled WMC's stock in the lead-up to the announcement, took the results well on Wednesday. The shares leapt 18 cents before settling at A$7.95, up 13 cents on Tuesday's close.
Analysts said that despite the disappointment of the first half, the global metals cycle was on the mend and investors were punting on better times ahead.
"I think the market will say: 'Bad half, it's behind us. The reality is now that metals are moving, therefore the profits should be up'," said Prudential-Bache Securities analyst Tony Robson.
He rated the stock a buy. "Effectively, you're buying in at the trough in profits."
Another analyst agreed: "Personally, I have a very positive outlook on the stock. I think the second half numbers will be a lot better."
Morgan said the company had accelerated the expansion of its giant Olympic Dam copper, uranium, gold and silver project in South Australia.
The expansion, which aims to double copper output at the mine, has been brought forward about a year to 1999 and now carries a total capital cost of A$1.48 billion.
The expansion was initially costed at A$1.25 billion.
